No genuine “conversation”—no logos—can develop out of such an answer.
Now ask the conscious proletarian why he gives part of his wages to a trade union or to the Party, even though doing so works against his immediate “vital” interests.
He can give an answer from which a conversation or an argument can begin: a long series of further questions and answers.

By distinguishing his true interests from merely temporary ones, and therefore acting according to reason (logos) against instinct, he immediately acquires both the gift of speech (logos) and the ability to ask and answer questions about his life and activity.
But the conscious proletarian knows more than this.
He knows not only his true interests, as distinct from his immediate biological ones, but also the effective means—the “method”—by which those interests can be realized.
Here too he is far more articulate, far more “logical,” than his unconscious comrade.
The latter certainly “knows,” for example, that if he wants to buy vodka he needs certain “means”: money, a shop, a shopkeeper, and so on.
But he knows this much as a cat “knows” that, in order to catch a mouse, it needs claws, must creep toward the hole from which the mouse may emerge, and so forth.
Ask the unconscious proletarian why money is necessary, and he will no longer be able to answer. He will fall silent immediately, or give what amounts to the same answer:
But ask the conscious proletarian why he needs money in order to contribute to a trade union, and he can give a fully rational answer:
“Because I live in a capitalist society, based on certain definite conditions…”
And that answer gives rise to another question and another reply.
But the conscious proletarian knows still more.
He knows not only the causes that make him act and the means by which he acts. He also knows his ultimate goal.
The unconscious proletarian frankly does not know what his life as a whole is for, and never even asks the question.
The conscious proletarian, by contrast, will immediately say that his whole life and all his activity are ultimately guided by the desire to help build communist society.
Such an answer will naturally open the way to a long conversation or argument.

It is especially important to notice that, at this point, the conscious proletarian goes beyond—“transcends”—not only the limits of his biological appetites but also the limits of his own actual life as a whole.

He strives toward a future society in which he will no longer exist physically and in which he will no longer exist socially either, since there will be no proletariat in a classless communist society.
So in answering questions about his own life and activity, he is inevitably forced to speak about human life and human activity in general.
He must therefore use the “abstract” concept of the human being—a concept abstracted from any particular individual—which only meaningful speech, logos, or reason can construct.
Of course, even the conscious proletarian will not be able to answer every question about his life and activity.
At some point he will inevitably fall silent or say, “I don’t know.”
But nothing follows from this except that, to use philosophical language, he is not yet a “sage.”

What is beyond doubt is that he strives toward wisdom. He tries to be able to answer as many of these vital questions as possible, and to live in such a way that his answers really are answers about his own life.
From this point of view, the “conscious proletarian” is no different from the “philosopher.”
What did the women who, at the beginning of the Russian Revolution, described themselves by saying “we are conscious”—a phrase that infuriated our enemies—actually mean?
First, they meant much the same thing as the proletarian who called himself “conscious.”
But there was also a more specific meaning in what these women said, and it completes the picture of revolutionary and socialist conscious awareness that we have just outlined.
By declaring themselves “conscious,” these women also meant that they had stopped thinking and repeating what men had told them about themselves.
Presocialist man had constructed a highly convenient image of woman, one that was far removed from what women actually were.
But men had succeeded so well in inserting this image into women’s own consciousness that women themselves had come to regard it as entirely accurate.
By rejecting this masculine image imposed on them—an image that did not correspond to what they really were—these “conscious women” were trying to speak about themselves, and to speak for themselves.

In other words, they moved away from a theological pseudo-philosophy in which “divine” men revealed to them what the “ideal woman” was supposed to be—an ideal woman who had never actually existed—and toward genuinely philosophical self-consciousness: their own consciousness of themselves.

The revolutionary and socialist call to “become conscious,” then, is identical with the genuinely philosophical call to self-consciousness: to knowledge that comes from the human being himself, not from “god,” and that concerns the human being himself, not “god.”

Like the philosopher, the revolutionary socialist tries to widen as far as possible the range of questions human beings can ask themselves about themselves and to provide as many convincing answers as possible.

How else are we to understand the fact that today, on Comrade Stalin’s personal initiative, the expansion of the revolutionary and socialist conscious awareness of the masses has been based on the study of the History of the Communist Party (Bolsheviks) of the USSR, which is then to be followed by the study of the history of the Union and finally of history in general?
This shows clearly that the purpose is not to “train” people or force them to live in some predetermined way.

On the contrary, the purpose is to teach them to live and act consciously, that is, rationally, so that they can give as many convincing answers as possible to questions about the way they live and act as members of the Party, citizens of the Union, and representatives of the most advanced part of humanity.
The study of the history of the Party, the Union, and the world is supposed to teach us to ask the broadest possible questions and give the best possible answers to the questions:
What does it mean to be a human being?
What does it mean to be a citizen of the Socialist Soviet Union?
What does it mean to be a member of the Communist Party?

It is therefore extremely important to notice that Stalin’s idea of introducing people to socialist revolution historically corresponds exactly to Hegel’s idea of providing a historical introduction to philosophy—an idea Hegel developed in his Phenomenology and that I have tried to take up again in this book.
Both rightly believe that we cannot understand the conscious awareness emerging in our own time unless we also take in the conscious awareness of the entire past.

Finally, the whole “scientific” socialism of Marx-Lenin-Stalin can be understood as a vast attempt to expand human conscious awareness to its natural limits and to give human beings the greatest possible ability to speak about themselves in a convincing and meaningful way.
For socialism does not stop with the present and the past. It also teaches us to speak rationally and convincingly about the future, and in doing so defines our ultimate goals.
Only then will it allow us to answer as fully and correctly as possible the question:
Having become conscious of the past, why do we live and act in the present in precisely this way rather than another?
For, as we will later see, full human awareness of the present—not merely biological but genuinely human awareness—includes elements belonging not only to the past but also to the future.

What has been said is enough to show that revolutionary socialism is closely connected with the concept of conscious awareness, which is indistinguishable from the philosophical concept of self-consciousness.
Genuine socialism therefore coincides with philosophy in the proper sense and has nothing in common with theological pseudo-philosophy.
Socialism consciously and rationally rejects every form of “revelation.”
Bourgeois and pre-bourgeois social and political doctrines, by contrast, ultimately make use of concepts such as the “sacred right of property,” “sacred rights of the individual,” and so on.
They do not always openly trace these principles back to divine revelation. But the fact that the adjective “sacred” so often appears here is anything but accidental.
We are dealing with principles that cannot be explained rationally. We reach questions before which we must either fall silent or submit to a superhuman—that is, “divine”—authority.
Socialism, by contrast, consciously seeks to ensure that all the concepts it uses are convincing: that they follow logically and discursively from other concepts found in ordinary human speech.
In any case, socialism recognizes no source of knowledge other than those available within human discourse.
Because it is radically atheistic, it obviously has nothing in common with theistic theology.
But it separates itself just as firmly from atheistic theology.

It repeatedly emphasizes that its knowledge is available to everyone, and that it is convincing not because Marx or some other “sage” or “saint” proclaimed it, but because everything Marx thought can be thought again by any human being capable of rational speech.
The same is true when socialism emphasizes its connection with real class interests.

By doing so, it shows that it addresses human beings in their normal conscious state. No special conditions are required in order to understand it—no conditions fundamentally different from those in which a human being ordinarily speaks about himself and his real life.
Revolutionary socialism, then, by rejecting every kind of theology, coincides exactly with what I have called philosophy in the proper sense.

When Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism claims that, in order to arrive inevitably at revolutionary socialism, we need only know ourselves—that is, actually know what we really are, or in other words know our real interests—it takes as the foundation of its doctrine the same self-consciousness that appears as the source, content, and goal of genuine philosophy.
But if socialism coincides with philosophy, then we should also find within socialism the same fundamental opposition that appears within philosophy as the opposition between theism and atheism.
As we have already said, this opposition comes down to whether the possibility of attaining wisdom is denied or affirmed.
And, as we will now see, this opposition does indeed appear within socialism.
Before turning to it, however, we need to say a few words about another problem closely connected with it.
The obvious fact that philosophy coincides with genuine socialism usually escapes the attention of thinkers for the following reason.
Suppose we grant that the ultimate goal of socialism and philosophy is the same.
Suppose the final ideal of both really is the complete realization of self-consciousness.
Even so, one might object, their means are completely different.
Socialism tries to reach this goal by changing the living conditions of humanity as a whole.
Philosophy relies only on the intellectual efforts of isolated individuals.
Socialism therefore takes the path of action toward a collective conscious awareness, whereas philosophy takes the individual path of inactive contemplation.
And we cannot say that an individual and contemplative enterprise is identical with an active and collective one.
But we already know that this claim is mistaken.
It is true that the individual and contemplative model applies to most philosophers.
It does not, however, characterize philosophy as such.

On the contrary, philosophy, in the course of its historical development, reached the conviction in Hegel—well before Marx—that self-consciousness, and even wisdom itself, is possible only under certain definite collective conditions.
In other words, the philosopher who strives toward wisdom is obliged to include within that striving all the politically conscious actions necessary to create those conditions.
So when Marx says that the path to self-consciousness includes not only intellectual and theoretical processes but also active political ones, he is simply following his teacher Hegel exactly.
Why this is so we will see later.
But even now we can say this much: if Marx is not to be counted as a philosopher, then Hegel must not be counted as one either.
And if, as everyone does, we include Hegel and Hegelianism within the history of philosophy, then we must include Marx and Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism as well.
